title: Sumedha in the mud
hookLine: a hermit lies down in the mud so the past Buddha Dipankara can walk over him, and vows to awaken (Jataka, the introduction)

cards: Mud. A stretch of road still soft and wet, and a Buddha walking toward it. The introduction to the Jataka opens long before Siddhartha, with a hermit named Sumedha.
A city is preparing its road for the Buddha Dipankara, and Sumedha has asked for a piece of it to make smooth himself. He hasn't finished. The mud is still there when Dipankara and his monks arrive.
So Sumedha does something nobody asked of him.

teach.h: FIRST HE GAVE IT ALL AWAY.
teach.b: First, who Sumedha was. In the story he's born rich. One day he looks at the treasure his family left him and thinks: they gathered all this, and not one of them took a coin along when they died.
So he gives it away and goes to the mountains to live as a hermit. The mud scene starts with empty hands. Second, the mud.

teach.h: HE LAY DOWN IN THE MUD.
teach.b: As Dipankara comes near, Sumedha loosens his hair, spreads his rough hermit's garment over the wet ground, and lies down in it, face down, so the Buddha and the monks can walk across him and keep their feet clean.
Not a speech. A body on a road. Third, the choice.
Lying there, the text says, Sumedha knows he could end his own suffering in this very life if he wished. He turns it down. What use is crossing over alone, he thinks.
He'd rather become a Buddha himself, and carry others across with him.
That's the vow: a longer road, chosen on purpose, for other people. Fourth, the answer.
Dipankara stops beside him, looks far ahead, and declares that this hermit will one day be a Buddha named Gotama. The crowd hears it.
Sumedha stands up. The Jataka's introduction sets the tales that follow on the long road from this vow. Mahayana traditions teach a bodhisattva vow too, in their own words and forms.
Here, the road begins with a man in the dirt, and a promise said silently.

how: In Theravada communities the story of Sumedha and Dipankara is told as the start of the Buddha's long path, and in Mahayana communities bodhisattva vows are taken in ceremonies and recited in practice.

o: a monk who has finished the path
a god who rules one of the heavens
one on the way to awakening, for others

games.q: the vow in the mud: tap the pairs.
p: the hermit who lay down in the mud
the past Buddha walking the road
he will be a Buddha named Gotama

s: Sumedha lay in the mud because his piece of the road wasn't finished
the mud was still there when Dipankara arrived, so he spread his garment and lay down in it.
Sumedha vowed to end his own suffering as fast as he could
the text says he could have, and turned it down to become a Buddha for others.
Sumedha's vow was a long, public speech to the crowd
he lay in the dirt and made it silently; Dipankara is the one who spoke.

games.q: you're Sumedha, face down in the mud. you know you could end your own suffering in this life. what do you choose?
o: end it now. it's what you came for.
vow to become a Buddha and carry others across.
get up and finish smoothing the road.
games.why: he turns down his own crossing and vows the longer road, and Dipankara declares he will one day be the Buddha Gotama.

practice: Choose one small vow you could actually keep, aimed at someone besides yourself: a little more room for one person, or patience with one message. Say it once, silently, the way Sumedha did in the mud, with nobody watching.
Then let it go and breathe; a vow can be quiet and still be real.

wordCard.voice: Bodhisatta. The being on the way to awakening: what Sumedha vowed to become when he lay down in the mud before the Buddha Dipankara, awakening not alone, but for others. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali bodhisatta: the being on the way to awakening. the tales use it for the future Buddha.

carryVoice: Your line: the vow in the mud. The longer road, chosen for others, starts with one quiet promise. Day eight hundred seventeen, done.
